hook: A 1963 policy memo from Maxwell W. Hunter II of the National Aeronautics and Space Council to the State Department's Office of International Scientific Affairs, exploring what U.S. diplomatic policy should be if alien intelligence were discovered — categorizing three hypothetical contact scenarios by their technological capability and prescribing different policy responses to each.
why_it_matters: This document reveals that senior U.S. government officials in the early space age were formally, if speculatively, thinking through alien contact as a policy problem requiring diplomatic preparation — not merely a scientific curiosity. The author explicitly frames the question of flying saucers and alien life as a matter with direct foreign-policy implications, depending on whether any discovered race possessed chemical, nuclear, or faster-than-light propulsion. The memo's candid conclusion — that policy would be made 'in the traditional manner of grand panic' because no one of consequence would take the question seriously until contact occurred — documents an awareness of institutional unpreparedness at the highest levels of the executive branch.

key_findings.finding: The document contains a significant date discrepancy: the metadata attributes it to 1952, but the document itself is dated July 18, 1963, and references events (Lunik III, Mariner II) that postdate 1952, confirming the correct year is 1963.

quotes.text: The other~side-of-the-moon pictures from Lunik III show no details of consequence, and the same can be said of the data from Mariner II compared to what we had already known about Venus from earth-based measurements.

key_findings.finding: The author categorizes potential alien contact into three policy-relevant tiers based on propulsion technology — chemical (primitive Martians), nuclear-capable (equivalent to humanity's best), or faster-than-light — and argues that U.S. diplomatic posture must differ drastically depending on which type is encountered.

quotes.text: Were we to find one, the question of whether it was a race with primitive chemical space flight, space flight equivalent to our best understanding of nuclear energy, or space flight based on physics beyond Einstein should be ascertained as rapidly as possible, since our policies would be affected in the most drastically possible way.
If we were to meet sucha race, our policy had better be to negotiate fast, because the implications of their far better understanding and control of the fundamental forces of nature would be obvious.

key_findings.finding: The author dismisses flying saucer advocates as credulous while simultaneously acknowledging that the scientific probability of extraterrestrial intelligence is finite and should not be entirely ignored, positioning himself between the two camps.

quotes.text: In my own mind, I find it difficult to side with the flying saucer advocates, but the almost total impossibility envisioned by most scientists also is disturbing.
Although all plausible scientific thinking suggests that we will not find any other intelligence race, the probability that we will is finite, and perhaps should not be completely ignored.

key_findings.finding: The memo analyzes three recent lunar and planetary anomalies that the author concedes would, in a less scientifically confident era, 'be hailed as broad hints of intelligent life on the moon' — including gas emissions from crater Alphonsus, infrared hot spots, and the repeated failures of deep space probes by both major spacefaring nations.

quotes.text: (1) The discovery of hot gasses eminating from the crater Alphonsus when the moon was supposedly dead. This would be considered evidence of civilization and, since Alphonsus is close to the visible edge, interpreted to mean that the other side of the moon was teaming with population which had begun

(3) The fact that no lunar or planetary probe of signi- ficance has been successful, in spite of major efforts on the part of two very successful earth orbitfaring nations. It would be supposed that someone was denying us deep space.

key_findings.finding: The memo's conclusion is pessimistic about institutional preparedness, explicitly predicting that because no one of consequence would take the alien question seriously in advance, U.S. policy would be improvised in a state of panic if contact actually occurred.

quotes.text: no one of consequence is going to take this rubbish seriously unless it happens. At that point, our policy will be determined in the traditional manner of grand panic.
the only body of writing on the subject available in an emergency is science fiction

legacy_program_connections.reasoning: The memo explicitly references nuclear energy as the upper bound of known propulsion capability and humorously imagines 'the Atomic Energy Commission of Mars,' reflecting the AEC's centrality to mid-century thinking about advanced technology and space capability.

The memo directly addresses the policy vacuum around UAP/alien contact preparedness, anticipating the same institutional gap that later bodies like AARO were created to address — and predicting it would remain unfilled until a forcing event.

As a formal policy memo from the Executive Office of the President to the State Department discussing alien contact as a matter of national diplomatic policy, it represents executive-branch engagement with questions that would later become subjects of congressional oversight.
